svg.title: Mining 12 production traces into a golden set: hard-case sampling versus random sampling
svg.desc: A support assistant's production log holds 12 traces, T01 through T12, each carrying two cheap free signals (the model's self-reported confidence and a guardrail or thumbs-down flag) while the true correct-or-failure label stays hidden until a human annotates it. A priority score of (1 minus confidence) plus 0.5 times flag ranks the traces from most to least suspicious: T12 at 1.10 down to T01 at 0.04. Of the 12 traces, 4 are true failures: T08, T09, T11, and T12, a true production failure rate of 4/12 = 0.33. Spending a budget of 6 annotations on the top 6 by priority (T12, T11, T10, T09, T08, T07) catches all 4 failures, a failure density of 0.67 and a coverage of 4/4 = 1.00. Spending the same budget of 6 on a fixed-seed random draw (T01, T04, T05, T07, T08, T12) catches only 2 failures, a density of 0.33 and a coverage of 2/4 = 0.50, matching the expected value of 6 times 4 over 12 = 2.00. Hard-case sampling is roughly twice as failure-dense as random. A three-round flywheel that annotates 2 hard cases per round grows a golden set of 6 traces: round 1 adds T12 and T11 for 2 new failures, cumulative coverage 0.50, gold rate 1.00; round 2 adds T10 and T09 for 1 new failure, cumulative coverage 0.75, gold rate 0.75; round 3 adds T08 and T07 for 1 new failure, cumulative coverage 1.00, gold rate 0.67. The closing note: the golden set's 0.67 failure rate is deliberately enriched and is not the true production rate of 0.33; an unbiased estimate of production health still needs a random holdout alongside the mined set.
